newsitem.title: USA: Calif. settles bond lawsuit against Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.headline: Calif. settles bond lawsuit against Goldman Sachs.

text.p: California said on Friday it reached a multi-million dollar agreement with Goldman Sachs & Co, settling a 1995 lawsuit over an ill-fated hospital deal financed with tax-exempt bonds.

Under the settlement, Goldman Sachs and its vice president, Vincent Forte, agreed to an initial cash payment of $28.5 million to California's Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development and the Attorney General's office.

The Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development would receive another $20 million, which would be paid by other defendants or by Goldman Sachs directly, according to the terms of the settlement.
Goldman Sachs also agreed to refinance the outstanding hospital bonds, ensuring that the state would realize saving of at least $8 million, the state said.
The agreement settled a lawsuit filed in February 1995 against Goldman Sachs and Forte. In entering into the settlement, neither Goldman Sachs nor Forte admitted to any wrongdoing.
The lawsuit arose out of the $142 million bond financing of two hospitals in southern California -- West Valley Community Hospital and Sherman Oaks Community Hospital.
The hospitals were owned by Nu-Med Corp, a for-profit hospital company. In 1990, they were acquired by a new non-profit corporation, called Triad Healthcare.
The Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development, through its Cal-Mortgage Loan Insurance Program, insured the debt financing that enabled Triad to buy the hospitals.
The Cal-Mortgage Program allows non-profit health facilities to benefit from the state's good credit ratings, and is backed by the full faith and credit of the state.
When Triad filed for bankruptcy in 1994, the state was left with the responsibility for most of the debt.
In response, the state sued Goldman Sachs and Forte, who represented both Nu-Med and Triad. The state alleged Goldman Sachs failed to fully disclose its role in the ill-fated deal.
The dispute prompted California state Treasurer Matt Fong to bar Goldman Sachs from acting as a financial adviser in any state treasury or authority transaction.
Goldman Sachs said it agreed to settle with the state to avoid the "expense and distraction of further litigation."
A spokesman for the firm said Goldman Sachs acted properly and was hopeful the settlement would mend its relationship with the state's treasurer.
The state said the settlement would benefit taxpayers.
"We are very pleased that Goldman Sachs chose to settle," said David Werdegar, director of the Office of Statewide Health Planning and Development.
"This is a major step forward toward restoring the losses incurred by the Cal-Mortgage Program in the Triad bankruptcy and reducing the financial risk to California taxpayers," he said.
The state's lawsuit against Goldman Sachs had sought $586 million from the firm.
